title: The bot that forgets
scenario: A startup shipped a support chat in a hurry. Users complain that the bot forgets what they said a minute ago. Finance also asks why long chats cost far more than short ones. You get the request log of one conversation (exhibit). Decide how the chat should handle messages.
exhibit:
conversation c-7781 (request log, input only)

turn 1  messages: [user "Hi, I'm Dana, order 5521 is late"]
         -> reply ok, stop_reason: end_turn
turn 2  messages: [user "Can you check it?"]
         -> reply: "Which order do you mean?"
turn 3  messages: [user "5521, I told you"]
         -> reply cut mid-sentence, stop_reason: max_tokens

max_tokens setting: 60

questions.prompt: In turn 2 the bot asks which order the user means. What is the root cause?

options.text: Each request sends only the newest user message.
options.explanation: Right. The API is stateless, so the app must send the earlier turns too. The Claude docs say the Messages API is stateless and you always send the full history; the OpenAI docs say each request stands alone and keeps no state.

options.text: The model's memory is full and needs a reset.
options.explanation: The model remembers nothing from one call to the next. Only what you send in the request exists for it.

options.text: The model forgot because the temperature is too high.
options.explanation: Sampling settings do not create or erase memory. Turn 1 was never sent again, so the model never saw it.

options.text: The user should repeat the order number in every message.
options.explanation: That pushes your system's job onto the user. The app should store and resend the conversation.

questions.prompt: Turn 3 ends mid-sentence with stop_reason max_tokens. What should the app do?

options.text: Treat the reply as cut off: raise max_tokens for this kind of answer, or continue it in another request.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs say max_tokens means the response reached your limit, and list two fixes: raise max_tokens or continue the response.

options.text: Show the reply as is. The model chose to stop there, so the answer must be complete.
options.explanation: end_turn is a natural stop; max_tokens is not. The model was cut off by your limit.

options.text: Retry the same request with the same settings until it ends normally, then keep the first complete reply.
options.explanation: The same 60-token cap will cut the answer again. Change the cap or continue the reply.

options.text: Ignore stop_reason. Only the text matters.
options.explanation: stop_reason is how you know whether the text is complete. Skipping it ships broken answers.

questions.prompt: The team moves to OpenAI and plans to use previous_response_id 'so old turns are free'. Is that right?

options.text: No. With previous_response_id, all previous input tokens in the chain are still billed as input.
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI conversation state guide says this in so many words. Linking by id saves resending, not paying.

options.text: Yes. The vendor stores the history on its side, so only the new message is billed as input tokens.
options.explanation: The OpenAI docs say the opposite: previous input tokens in the chain are billed as input.

options.text: Yes, but only for the first 10 turns.
options.explanation: There is no such rule in the docs. The full chain is billed as input.

options.text: No, because previous_response_id is not a real parameter.
options.explanation: It is a documented way to share context across responses. The issue is the billing, not the parameter.

questions.prompt: Finance asks why turn 40 of a chat costs much more than turn 2, even for a short question. Which answer is correct?

options.text: Every turn resends the history, so input tokens grow as the conversation grows.
options.explanation: Right. A stateless API needs the full history each call, so later turns carry more input tokens.

options.text: Vendors charge a higher price per token late in a conversation.
options.explanation: The price per token does not depend on the turn number. The number of tokens grows.

options.text: Late turns use a bigger model under the hood, so they cost more per token and per call.
options.explanation: The model does not change by turn. The input grows because the history is resent.

options.text: Short questions cost more because they need more thinking.
options.explanation: Question length is not the driver here. The resent history is.
